name: statement-equivalence/strict
says: For asking whether two statements state the same information, with the careful reader answering the questions that decide.

events.by: Claude (Fable 5.2), a draft for the repo owner to ratify or replace
events.says: Two figures are the same figure when the readers value them equally and the same sign or unit mark is written against them ("-5" is not "5"; "$500" is not "€500"). A figure nobody valued is matched only by the same written form. A name is the same name when it is spelled the same, letter case kept. A figure or a name with no equal is always asked about, whatever the whole reading said. Whether two texts are about one particular thing is asked of a reader, both ways round, and is never assumed from shared words or from the texts being identical.

events.by: Claude (Fable 5.2), a draft for the repo owner to ratify or replace
events.says: Letter case, spacing, and compatibility forms of a character (a ligature, a full-width digit) are accidental and are not followed. Every other token is followed, marks included: a currency sign, a minus sign and a question mark are places two texts can part. In English, the readers' own tags may decide one thing without asking anyone: a pair that parts only by a negation and its auxiliary. No reordering is decided by tags under this ground: every reordering goes to a reader.

events.by: Claude (Fable 5.2), a draft for the repo owner to ratify or replace
events.says: A stated time or tense is a statement like any other. Two texts that differ in when are different in what they state. This kernel has no other time rule.

events.by: Claude (Fable 5.2), a draft for the repo owner to ratify or replace
events.says: What one text states and the other does not is a difference, for the side the question asks about. A reader that gives no answer leaves a gap, never a yes or a no. When a whole text is not carried, the quick reader is asked whether the other text is opposed to it or only silent.

events.by: Claude (Fable 5.2), a draft for the repo owner to ratify or replace
events.says: "No difference" may stand alone only if each whole text was read against the other; a question shaped without that reading cannot be closed as "no difference" under this ground. The finder walks back to say where only when a whole text is not carried. Once one direction is not carried the other is not asked, and once a mechanical difference survives the whole texts are not asked: in both cases the answer could not change. Limits: texts sharing fewer than half their tokens in order are read part by part, not place by place; at most 3 places are asked one by one, 12 parts, and 6 figures or names, and 4 surviving parts are typed; whatever is beyond a limit is left open and said so. A part that is 85% of its text is the text again and is not asked twice. An identity question may stand as "the same thing" alone only if a control statement was asked about too.

events.by: Claude (Fable 5.2), a draft for the repo owner to ratify or replace
events.says: The words of every question are the same as in the casual ground. What makes this the stricter baseline is who answers: whole texts, single places and figures are read by the deliberate reader (the model with its thinking on). Measured on development pairs, that reader refused most texts that add or change one fact, and also refused about a quarter of true paraphrases. Parts, names, the same-thing question and the kind question are read by the quick reader, so for those two questions this ground and the casual one are the same ground.

questions.system: You are a careful reader. Answer only from the PASSAGE. Do not use outside knowledge.
questions.says: Does the passage say that the sentence is true? Answer yes only if the passage states it or it follows directly from what the passage states.
questions.part: Does the passage say what the PART of the sentence says? Answer yes only if the passage states it or it follows directly from what the passage states.
questions.figure: Does the passage give the same figure as the PART, written in digits or in words? Answer yes only if the passage gives that exact figure. A vaguer amount (more than, about, several) is not the same figure.
questions.mentions: Does the passage mention or refer to what the PART names, in any wording? Answer yes or no.
questions.denies: Does the passage say that the sentence is false? Answer yes only if the passage states the opposite of the sentence or something that cannot be true together with it.
questions.about: Are the PASSAGE and the SENTENCE about the same particular thing, event or rule, whether or not they agree about it? Answer yes or no.
questions.kind: Is the PASSAGE itself of the KIND named? Answer yes only if the passage is one. A passage that merely mentions or describes one is not one.
